node.label: Carroll Smith-Rosenberg
node.date_label: The Female World of Love and Ritual (1975) · Disorderly Conduct (1985) · The Body Politic (1989) · This Violent Empire (2010)
node.description: In “The Female World of Love and Ritual” (1975), Carroll Smith-Rosenberg closely analysed the emotional, and arguably sexual, intimacy recorded in nineteenth-century American women’s letters, treating sexuality as fluid and shaped by cultural and social forces rather than settling whether these women were lesbians. Disorderly Conduct (1985) collected her essays on gender and sexuality. A 2021 OutHistory interview report calls the article pathbreaking, and Penn’s women’s studies programme credits it with establishing the legitimacy of lesbian history. The article came under intense criticism in the 1980s: by the interview report’s account, some scholars thought it essentialist for suggesting that the women might be understood as lesbian, while others thought it glorified chaste passions between women. Smith-Rosenberg also became an acknowledged resource for Spiegel’s social reading of texts. This Violent Empire (2010), in its publisher’s account, traced American national identity through exclusions that accompanied the republic’s founding.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “The Female Animal” (1973), with Charles Rosenberg; “The Female World of Love and Ritual” (1975); Disorderly Conduct: Visions of Gender in Victorian America (1985, Knopf); “The Body Politic” (1989); “Dis-Covering the Subject of the ‘Great Constitutional Discussion,’ 1786–1789” (1992); This Violent Empire: The Birth of an American National Identity (2010; paperback 2012).
node.scope_note: The 1975 article and Kerber (1988) could not be read on a permitted route; their characterization rests on the 2021 OutHistory interview report and Penn’s biography. Spiegel (1993), acknowledgments xi–xiii, introduction selected pp. 9–10 and note 7; Hall (1992), p. 117 and note 4. Newman’s selected discussion and the 2021 interview report read. The 1973 coauthored article and 1989 forum were checked for publication credit only. Disorderly Conduct, The Body Politic, the constitutional article and This Violent Empire were not read in full; the latter book’s argument is identified through its publisher. No original archival letters independently checked.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Romancing the Past (1993), Spiegel credits Smith-Rosenberg’s sustained manuscript reading and uses “The Body Politic” (1989) in explaining the social setting of textual meaning.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh official UC Press/CDL text: acknowledgments xiii, introduction 9–10 and introduction n. 7, p. 325. Spiegel says Smith-Rosenberg “read every chapter”; n. 7 identifies the 1989 essay, p. 101, and thanks her for the draft. Remaining chapters and the original essay unread. Direction records Spiegel’s expressed debt; does not transfer her medieval conclusions to Smith-Rosenberg.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 1986 review of Carroll Smith-Rosenberg’s Disorderly Conduct: Visions of Gender in Victorian America (1985), Linda Gordon criticized the treatment of sexual concerns as metaphors for other social conflicts and questioned the usefulness of its expansive application of liminality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s licensed first-page image preview, first by in-memory OCR and then visually checked against the image. The landing page identifies Gordon as reviewer and dates the review to September 1986. On p. 477 she questions reducing sexual issues to symbols of other concerns, then argues that an application of liminality broad enough to encompass most nineteenth-century experience limits its usefulness. Gordon also praises Smith-Rosenberg’s close reading and earlier work; the proposal concerns these specified criticisms, not blanket rejection. The review continues on p. 478, which remains unread. The web image fetch failed, but a normal direct request to the same publisher-supplied preview image returned HTTP 200. No full-review access is claimed.
